text:
Anyone can make an assertion without evidence but then why didn't Leo Frank and his attorney's put that  alleged event in their appeals to the defense-friendly trial judge or higher courts? It would have been grounds to get their client a new trial. 

If the Jury Was Threatened, Why Didn't Leo Frank's Lawyers Use It?

If a mob really shouted “Hang the Jew,” in the trial as Arthur Burton Rascoe asserted 16 months after the trial, or threatened Leo Frank’s jurors with death unless they convicted the defendant, one question is hard to avoid: 

Why did Frank and his lawyers fail to use such an event while trying to stop the trial, throw out the guilty verdict, and win another trial?

Frank’s lawyers did complain about crowd behavior.

The defense complained about an applause by someone inside the courtroom, cheering outside the courthouse, and cries of “Hurrah for Dorsey.” 

The defense put these complaints into the official legal record, called witnesses about them, gathered sworn affidavits, used the issue in Frank’s request for another trial, and they carried his case to the Supreme Court of Georgia. Yet the later story about a mob threatening the jurors with “Hang the Jew,” or “Hang the Jew or we’ll hang you,” does not appear in these 1913 complaints. It doesn't appear in the three competing Atlanta newspapers. It doesn't appear in anything Rosser, or Arnold stated or wrote. It was a hoax fabricated in Chicago, the birth place of the ADL, the place where Albert Lasker was one of the primary "angel" investors of the Frank defense campaign, which I and others write about extensively. 

What Was a Motion for a Mistrial?

A motion is a formal request asking a judge to do something. A motion for a mistrial asks the judge to stop a trial while it is still going on because a serious problem has supposedly made a fair trial impossible going further.

On Monday, August 25, 1913, after Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey finished his closing argument, Frank’s attorney Reuben Arnold asked Judge Leonard S. Roan to declare a mistrial. The jury was removed from the courtroom while Arnold made his request. The Atlanta Journal described Arnold’s request as a formal motion for a mistrial and listed the crowd incidents he relied upon (Atlanta Journal, 1).

Arnold complained about applause inside the courtroom and cheering outside the courthouse. He referred to Friday, August 22, 1913, when a crowd reportedly cheered Dorsey after court recessed, and Saturday, August 23, 1913, when another demonstration occurred as Dorsey left the courthouse. Arnold said people cried “Hurrah for Dorsey” while the jury was nearby. He also complained about applause for Dorsey on Monday, August 25, 1913, while jurors were in a nearby room.

Judge Roan acknowledged hearing some cheering, although he said he did not hear the words “Hurrah for Dorsey.” Bailiffs were questioned. Some admitted hearing noise or cheering, while others said they did not hear the words Arnold reported. Arnold himself testified about what he heard. 

Yet, the surviving reports do not give us a reliable headcount or identify every person who joined the cheering, so we shouldn't pretend to know who every person in the crowd was. We don't know how many, where they were, or if they were working subrosa for the defense. There's always the possibly they were a plant that was staged to generate the incident. The defense had allegedly planted much evidence against Newt Lee, the death notes, the time card alteration, the blood soaked shirt. It's not beyond the realm of possibilities that the cheering was generated by the defense, but like everything there needs to be evidence for or against to sustain, or argue or debate something. 

Arnold argued these public demonstrations could intimidate or influence the jury. Judge Roan denied the mistrial request, gave the jury its legal instructions, and sent the jurors out to decide the case. The jury returned a guilty verdict later on August 25, 1913.

What Does “Preserved in the Record” Mean?

When I say Frank’s lawyers “preserved” the “Hurrah for Dorsey” complaint, I mean they placed it into the official court record. A court record is the collection of testimony, motions, rulings, affidavits, and other papers used in a court case.

This defense action is important because a higher court normally reviews what happened in the lower court by reading this record. If a lawyer wants a higher court to review an alleged error, the lawyer usually needs to raise the issue and make sure a written record exists showing what supposedly happened. The Georgia Supreme Court's tribunal reviewed this record and other defense motions from November 1913 all through 1914 at various stages and episodes. 

Frank’s lawyers did exactly this with the crowd complaints. Arnold raised the issue in court on August 25, 1913. Witnesses were questioned about the cheering. After Frank was convicted, his lawyers gathered affidavits about crowd behavior and again used public demonstrations as part of their effort to get another trial after the adverse verdict.

So when we ask why the defense preserved the comparatively mild cry of “Hurrah for Dorsey,” this is where it was preserved: in Frank’s own court proceedings and in the legal papers used to challenge his conviction.

What Was a Motion for a New Trial?

A motion for a new trial is different from a motion for a mistrial. A mistrial request asks a judge to completely stop a trial while it is still underway, not pause it, but end it. A motion for a new trial is made after the jury has returned a verdict. It asks the judge to throw out the old verdict and hold another trial.

Frank’s lawyers filed a motion for a new trial after his conviction. They later expanded it with more than one hundred claimed errors or reasons for another trial. Lawyers often call each separate legal reason a ground. In plain English, a ground is simply one reason offered to the judge for granting a new trial. Judge Roan rejected all 100+ grounds. The judge refused a new trial for Leo Frank after giving the defense an opportunity to present a long document of alleged errors on paper and orally argue their perspective.

The crowd complaint did not disappear. Frank’s lawyers again raised applause, cheering, public demonstrations, and possible influence on the jury. They supplied affidavits from people who claimed to have seen or heard some of these events and argued the public atmosphere around the courthouse had hurt Frank’s right to a fair trial.

Judge Roan heard the arguments and reviewed the large amount of material presented by the defense. On Friday, October 31, 1913, he denied Frank’s motion for a new trial. Frank’s lawyers then took the case to the Supreme Court of Georgia (Atlanta Georgian, 3).

So Where Is the Alleged Death Threat?

This is where the later “Hang the Jew” confabulation becomes difficult to fit into the 1913 legal record. Frank’s lawyers preserved complaints about applause, cheers for Dorsey, the location of jurors, the distance between jurors and crowds, and arguments over what the jurors might have heard.

If people openly threatened to kill or lynch jurors unless they convicted Frank, such an incident would have been far more serious than people shouting “Hurrah for Dorsey.” It would have supported the exact argument Arnold was already making. Frank’s defense was claiming outside public pressure could intimidate the jury and damage Frank’s right to a fair trial.

Yet the 1913 legal material discussed here does not show Arnold telling Judge Roan about a mob shouting “Hang the Jew” at the jury. The defense material concerning crowd demonstrations discussed here does not supply such a threat either. Frank’s lawyers documented far smaller demonstrations, but this much more serious alleged death threat is missing.

Its absence does not prove nobody in Atlanta ever made an antisemitic remark. It does not prove every spectator behaved properly. The narrower historical question is much easier to state: Where is the contemporary evidence for a mob threatening Frank’s jurors with death unless they convicted him? 

Where are the affidavits? Where are the courtroom eyewitnesses who said they heard these alleged antisemitic death threats? Where is the police report? Where is any complaint from Frank’s lawyers to Judge Leonard Roan saying jurors had been threatened with violence?

Where are the reports from the police officers and bailiffs who guarded the jurors and escorted them between the courthouse and their rooms at the Kimball House? Where are the Atlanta newspaper reports describing a mob shouting “Hang the Jew” at the jury? Where, in Frank’s motion for a mistrial, his motion for a new trial, the supporting affidavits, or his appeals, do his lawyers describe such a threat?

Frank’s defense complained about applause. They complained about cheering for Solicitor General Hugh Dorsey. They preserved cries of “Hurrah for Dorsey.” They gathered affidavits about crowd noise and argued jurors might have heard it.

Yet they did not raise a supposed “Hang the Jew” death threat. That's doubtful if it actually happened.

No comparable 1913 legal record has been produced showing Frank’s lawyers complained to the judge or any judge (state or federal Supreme Court tribunal) about such a threat, reported it to police, obtained affidavits from eyewitnesses, or used it as a reason for another trial.

Instead, the dramatic story appears later, far away from Atlanta, in a newspaper published hundreds of miles away in Chicago, Illinois, on the shore of Lake Michigan, one of the Great Lakes shared by the United States and Canada. And it was invented a year and four months after the trial ended by a young journalist two years out of college and building a career.

If such a serious threat really occurred within hearing of the jury, the obvious historical question remains: 

Why is it missing from the contemporary legal record created by the very lawyers searching for evidence of jury intimidation?

The Georgia Supreme Court Reviewed the Evidence

Frank’s appeal went to the Supreme Court of Georgia, the highest state court in Georgia. On February 17, 1914, the court affirmed Frank’s conviction by a vote of 4 to 2 in Frank v. State, 141 Ga. 243, 80 S.E. 1016 (Georgia Supreme Court, 4).

To say the court affirmed the conviction means the higher court allowed the conviction and judgment to remain in place. The court did not hold another murder trial. Its job was to review the legal record, examine Frank’s claims of error, and decide whether the law required another trial.

Another important legal phrase is sufficiency of the evidence. It simply means whether enough legal evidence existed for a jury to reach the verdict it reached. It does not mean every justice had to believe every witness, nor does it mean the Supreme Court held a second trial and decided all of the facts again.

The four-justice majority expressly said it had carefully considered the evidence and found the evidence sufficient to uphold the verdict. The majority also found no substantial error requiring another trial. In other words, four justices directly rejected the argument claiming the trial evidence was legally too weak to support Frank’s conviction.

Two justices dissented, Chief Justice William H. Fish and Justice Hiram Warner Beck. A dissent is an opinion written by judges who disagree with the majority on one or more legal questions. Fish and Beck disagreed with the majority mainly over evidence concerning Frank’s alleged prior sexual conduct, including testimony from Jim Conley and C. B. Dalton. They believed some of this evidence should not have been admitted for the jury to hear.

But Fish and Beck did not say the evidence in the murder case was legally insufficient to support the conviction. Their dissent attacked certain evidence admitted during the trial. They did not write an opinion saying the State had failed to present enough evidence for a guilty verdict. No justice on the Georgia Supreme Court wrote an opinion declaring the trial evidence legally insufficient.

Frank’s lawyers then asked the Supreme Court of Georgia for a rehearing. A rehearing is a request asking the same court to look at its decision again. The disagreement between the justices over the evidence issue remained, but all six justices agreed to deny Frank’s request for a rehearing.

This does not mean every justice agreed on every legal question. They plainly did not. But it is important when discussing later claims of an unfair trial. The majority found the evidence sufficient to support the verdict, and the two dissenters based their disagreement on the admission of certain evidence rather than a finding of legally insufficient evidence.

Why “Hurrah for Dorsey” Is Important

“Hurrah for Dorsey” is important in the spectrum of complaints, precisely, because it was not a death threat. Frank’s lawyers considered ordinary cheering important enough to document because they hoped to show improper public influence on the jury. Read that again, a solicitor being cheered as he walks out of court was considered significant enough for the defense to raise it as evidence why Leo Frank deserved a new trial. 

They identified dates, locations, noise, distances, applause, and witnesses. They argued about whether jurors could hear the demonstrations. They raised these complaints in the August 25, 1913 mistrial fight and again during their effort to win another trial.

If a direct death threat against the jurors had occurred within their hearing, it would have been much stronger evidence for the same defense argument. Yet the dramatic antisemitic lynching ultimatum found in later accounts is absent from the contemporary crowd complaints examined here.

The Later Story Becomes Much More Dramatic

A much stronger version appeared later during the public campaign to save Frank from execution. 

On Sunday, December 27, 1914, about sixteen months after the verdict, Burton Rascoe published a long article in the Chicago Sunday Tribune. Rascoe claimed men in the courtroom distracted jurors by shouting a warning telling them they had better hang Frank or face violence themselves (Chicago Sunday Tribune, 5). The article by Rascoe reads as if it were written by a crazed fanatic with no pretense of objectivity. In one sentence he's raving about Jew hatred, in another, he's dehumanizing a Negro witness, without any self awareness for the irony of complaining about bigotry or prejudice. Read the article, it's in the references. There's an audiobook on the same page if anyone is too lazy to read the text.

This later account raises basic source questions. Who shouted the threat? On what day did it happen? Where was the speaker standing? Which juror heard it? Which Atlanta newspaper reported it in 1913? Which defense lawyer raised it? Which affidavit recorded it? Where does it appear in Frank’s mistrial request or new-trial papers? Who? What? When? Where? How? and, Why? That's how we trace evidence. We look at when it emerged, and who brought it forward. Was it a radical pro-Frank activist? Does their writing reflect objectivity? Parts of Burton Rascoe's article could just as easily been published in a KKK Ku Klux Klan newsletter the way he wrote it with such extreme partisanship. The defense lawyers used the same language and worse, it was a tirade of racial invective, meant to fool the jury, but the saw right through the BS.  Skin color could not be used as a race card or a White privilege card to trump testimony, physical and circumstantial evidence. The jury voted on the evidence, not on Klan rhetoric, not on false accusations of antisemitism, Jew-hatred or religious prejudice. Most thinking people can not be manipulated with such tribal extremism over evidence.  Justice was more important than race is how the jury decided. Truth was more important than tribe. 

These questions become more important because the 1913 defense record is not silent about crowd conduct. 

Frank’s lawyers preserved lesser demonstrations in detail. The problem is not an absence of crowd complaints. The problem is the absence of this particular death-threat story from legal proceedings built, in part, around claims of outside pressure on the jury.

Blog: The Origin and Growth of the “Hang the Jew” Story

The Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project has a much longer source study devoted to this claim: 

“Notorious or Infamous? The Antisemitic Death Threat Hoax: ‘Hang the Jew, or We’ll Hang You!’” 

The research study traces changing versions of the story from the original period through later newspaper, magazine, book, and internet accounts and compares later claims with the earlier legal record (Mary Phagan Kean Legacy Project, 6).

The article also explains citogenesis and citation laundering. 

Citogenesis happens when repeated copying makes a claim look well established even when later writers may all be repeating the same earlier source. 

Citation laundering happens when a weak or poorly supported claim passes through later books and articles until readers have difficulty seeing how little support existed at the beginning.

The dates are especially important for the chronology and timing reference. In August 1913, Frank’s lawyers documented applause, cheering, and alleged cries of “Hurrah for Dorsey.” In October 1913, they used claims of unfair influence while asking Judge Roan for another trial. On February 17, 1914, the Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the conviction, with the majority expressly finding sufficient evidence to uphold the verdict. The much more dramatic published story of jurors being openly threatened with violence appears later.
